topics.title: New exposure, or new visibility?
topics.subtitle: Why a bigger number is not always worse news

turns.text: Cole, the finding count jumped this week. Should the team panic?
Not yet. First ask where the new findings came from. If they're on machines we've been scanning all along, that's new exposure. Something changed, and it needs a look.
But if they're on machines we only just started scanning, or just gave the scanner credentials for, that's new visibility. The risk was already there. We can finally see it.
So a higher number can actually mean better coverage.
Exactly. And the reverse is the trap. When a finding disappears from a machine that missed its scan, that's not a fix. It's unverified until a rescan proves it.
New exposure, new visibility, verified fixed, unverified. Four different stories, and this station keeps them apart for you.

topics.title: EPSS in sixty seconds
topics.subtitle: What the exploit prediction score does and does not tell you

turns.text: You'll hear us mention EPSS. Cole, what is it, in plain English?
It's the Exploit Prediction Scoring System, run by FIRST. Every day it estimates the chance that a vulnerability sees exploitation activity somewhere in the next thirty days.
So a high score means we're about to get hacked?
No, and that's the common mistake. It describes activity across the internet, not the odds that your environment gets breached. It's a signal for ordering work.
Use it alongside CISA's known exploited list, which tells you attacks are already happening, and alongside what the asset actually does for the business.
Known exploited first, then likely to be exploited, then everything else. That's a plan a small team can actually follow.

topics.title: What CISA's exploited list really tells you
topics.subtitle: The strongest public signal that attackers are using a bug

turns.text: Every briefing starts with CISA's known exploited list. Why does it get top billing?
Because it's evidence, not a prediction. CISA only adds a vulnerability when there's reliable proof it's being exploited and there's clear guidance to fix it.
And it's not just for government agencies?
Agencies get formal deadlines. For everyone else, it's free, it updates often, and it's the shortest list of things attackers are using right now.
So when something on that list shows up on one of our machines, it jumps the queue.
Every time. That's why the station will interrupt the music for it.
